extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners before the USPTO (trademark attorneys), OED/USPTO officials, and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, evidentiary burdens, and sanctioning criteria applied in a USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline administrative disciplinary proceeding concerning trademark-practice misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO disciplinary authority (35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has the 'exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it.' The Director may suspend or exclude a person if shown to be 'incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or for violating Office regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary action under 35 U.S.C. § 32 requires notice and opportunity for a hearing; proceedings follow USPTO procedural rules and APA section 7 (5 U.S.C. § 556) and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.39, 11.44.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; Respondent bears the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is an intermediate standard 'between a preponderance of the evidence and proof beyond a reasonable doubt.' It requires evidence 'of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy.' Evidence is clear if 'certain, unambiguous, and plain' and convincing if 'reasonable and persuasive enough' to cause belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101 et seq.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO promulgated disciplinary rules modeled on the ABA Model Rules, effective May 3, 2013, which apply to persons practicing before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules supply the substantive duties (e.g., diligence, communication) and the framework for practitioner responsibilities and sanctions used by the OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS signature requirement (37 C.F.R. § 2.193(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: All forms filed with TEAS must be personally signed; it is not permissible for a person to sign another person’s name to a TEAS form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TEAS offers multiple signature methods (ESIGN-ON, DIRECT, and pen-and-ink) to facilitate personal signatures; misuse of these methods (e.g., third parties entering a client's signature improperly) violates USPTO requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESIGN-ON signature method description
rubrics_metrics.description: ESIGN-ON allows a preparer to send a link to a third party who opens the link, reviews the filing, and electronically enters their signature (between two forward slashes); the originator then accesses the electronically signed document and submits it to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is typically used to obtain client signatures (e.g., firms sending the form to clients). Evidence that ESIGN-ON was used supports that a third party legitimately affixed the signatory's signature if corroborated by logs/emails.

rubrics_metrics.name: DIRECT signature method description and evidentiary implication
rubrics_metrics.description: The DIRECT method is the default: the originator completes the TEAS form and personally enters their electronic signature between two forward slashes. When using DIRECT, the computer used to sign must be the same one used to file the document; if a form is saved and later uploaded, previously affixed DIRECT signatures are removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: XML/TEAS data for DIRECT signatures includes the IP address of the computer that both signed and filed; matching signature-entry and filing IP address is evidence the signatory personally entered the signature or was physically present when it was entered. If a DIRECT-signed filing shows a single IP address for multiple geographically dispersed clients, it strongly suggests signatures were not personally entered by those clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner supervisory duty regarding non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners having direct supervisory authority over a non-practitioner assistant shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the person's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner is also responsible for misconduct of a non-practitioner assistant if the practitioner has direct supervisory authority. Reasonable efforts include oversight of assistant practices and ensuring signature/filing methods comply with USPTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner responsibility for actions they cause or authorize
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may be implicated if they prepare, review, cause to be prepared, or cause to be filed trademark documents (even if another attorney is nominally the attorney of record).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being the attorney of record, preparing initial filings, approving drafts, or otherwise causing filings to be submitted can establish responsibility for ensuring filings comply with signature and filing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations: failure to act with reasonable diligence (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation occurs when a practitioner leaves important tasks to non-practitioner assistants without adequately supervising them or ensuring they carry out duties appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include delegating collection of client signatures and filing to assistants without confirming methods used; negligence in oversight supports finding of § 11.103 violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations: failure to reasonably communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner violates communication rules by not informing clients when there is a likelihood their trademark filings were affected by impermissible signature practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even absent proof of misconduct, reasonable communication after learning of possible client-impacting issues is required; delaying or failing to notify clients can be a separate violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for OED complaints (35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplinary proceeding must be commenced not later than the earlier of (a) 10 years after the date on which the misconduct occurred, or (b) one year after the date on which the misconduct is made known to an office or employee of the Office; USPTO rules more specifically require a complaint be filed within one year after the OED Director receives a grievance forming the basis of the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'grievance' is a 'written submission from any source received by the OED Director that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1). The respondent bears the burden to prove a statute-of-limitations affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of TEAS/TICRS/XML/IP address data as evidentiary metric
rubrics_metrics.description: TEAS/TICRS/XML data can show the signature method used (DIRECT vs ESIGN-ON) and collect the IP address from which the filing was submitted; TEAS also generates filing receipts with TEAS Stamps recording start/end times and IP addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This data can be used to infer whether clients themselves entered signatures (DIRECT+matching geographically appropriate IP) or whether signatures were entered from a small set of IP addresses inconsistent with client locations. Caution: external geolocation sources (e.g., public 'what is my IP' websites) require foundation/corroboration before being deemed reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence weight and reliability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony, declarations, emails, settlement agreements, and XML/exhibit data are assessed for relevance, directness, and corroboration; uncorroborated declarations or internet-based geolocation printouts may be given limited weight absent foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court assesses whether exhibits relate directly to the specific filings at issue; documents suggesting a firm's general practice are probative but do not substitute for direct evidence tying the practitioner to the specific misconduct without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and assessment of negligence vs. intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Negligence is 'the failure to take reasonable care.' The practitioner's mental state (intentional, knowing, or negligent) affects sanction analysis; negligent conduct supports sanction but may militate against the most severe penalties reserved for intentional or knowing misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant facts include whether the practitioner followed firm procedures, whether they made reasonable inquiries when concerns arose, and whether there is evidence of conscious avoidance or knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary purpose of discipline is protection of the public and bar, not punishment. The Court often consults the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions and seeks proportionality between violation and penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common aggravating and mitigating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors can include a pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, substantial experience in the field, and refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing; mitigating factors can include long career with no prior discipline, genuine remorse, and cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court evaluates the record to identify applicable aggravators/mitigators (e.g., repeated negligent filings over months = pattern; no prior discipline = mitigation) and weighs them in determining an appropriate sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of sanctions and typical remedial outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions should be proportionate to the violation; protection of the public is paramount. For negligent but non-egregious misconduct, lesser sanctions such as public reprimand and probation may be appropriate instead of suspension or exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example outcome here: public reprimand and twelve-month probation found sufficient where misconduct was negligent, not intentional, no evidence of actual client injury, and mitigating factors existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner obligation to investigate and remediate upon learning of firm-wide issues
rubrics_metrics.description: When made aware of possible improper practices (e.g., impermissible signature use by firm assistants), practitioners have an obligation to make reasonable inquiries, supervise delegated matters, and communicate with clients where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to inquire of assistants, failing to obtain access to firm systems that would clarify whether clients signed, and declining to inform clients until 'proof' is obtained are identified as insufficient; reasonable steps should be taken once concerns arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence needed to sustain an affirmative statute-of-limitations defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The respondent must prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that the misconduct forming the basis for the proceeding was 'made known' (a grievance received) more than one year before the complaint was filed or that more than ten years have passed since the misconduct occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstantial inferences about OED knowledge are considered, but the respondent must produce direct or strong circumstantial evidence showing when a grievance was received by the OED in relation to the complaint filing date.
